title: Deliver a Tough Message in the First Two Sentences
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article prescribes a specific structural technique for delivering unpopular decisions: state the 'why' in the first sentence and the resulting action or outcome in the second, rather than easing into the message. The reasoning is that clarity, not gentleness, is what produces respect and prevents misinterpretation — and that leaders who 'think their way through' a tough message in real time tend to create confusion instead. The piece distinguishes this from situations where a decision hasn't actually been made yet, in which case exploratory listening is the right approach instead. Several scripted examples illustrate the why-then-action formula in practice.
points: The core technique is structural: state the reason in sentence one and the concrete action/outcome in sentence two, front-loading the hard part instead of building up to it.
The stated goal is clarity, not softness — the article explicitly argues that easing into bad news produces more pain for both parties, not less.
The technique is scoped to already-made decisions; when a decision is still open, the article recommends exploratory listening instead of the why-then-action formula.
quotes: If there is good advice about delivering a tough message, it goes like this: The bad news must come up front — in the first two sentences.
The first sentence explains the why, and the second sentence states the action or outcome.
Far too often, leaders “think” their way through a tough message and create a mess in the process.
Waiting to get to the point is akin to ripping off the band-aid slowly. It is usually much more painful for both parties.
If the decision or action can’t be negotiated, then a leader’s integrity won’t let it unfold any other way.
